intro: This topic covers choosing and using contraception (including the UKMEC eligibility rules), emergency contraception, abortion and the first steps in infertility care. The AMC tests the safest and most effective method for a given woman, drug interactions, time limits for emergency contraception, state-based abortion law and conscientious objection, and consent and confidentiality for young people.

lessons.title: Choosing contraception: effectiveness, UKMEC and consent
objectives: Rank contraceptive methods by typical-use effectiveness and explain why LARC is first line
Apply the UKMEC categories to decide whether a woman can safely use combined hormonal contraception
Take a contraceptive history that covers medical eligibility, drugs and preferences
Assess a young person's capacity to consent to contraception confidentially

sections.heading: The Australian approach
sections.body:
About half of pregnancies in Australia are unplanned, and many occur in women using a short-acting method imperfectly. The key idea is **typical use** versus **perfect use**: methods that depend on daily action (the pill) or action at every act of sex (condoms) fail far more often in real life than on paper. **Long-acting reversible contraception (LARC)** removes user error, so Australian guidance (RANZCOG, RACGP, Family Planning / Sexual Health organisations) recommends offering LARC **first line to all women, including adolescents and nulliparous women**.

Australia uses the **UK Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use (UKMEC)** to decide which methods are safe for which medical conditions. Contraception is also a consent and confidentiality topic: young people frequently present alone.

sections.heading: Effectiveness and the methods available
sections.body:
Approximate percentage of women with an unintended pregnancy in the **first year of typical use**:

| Method | Typical-use failure | Duration / notes |
|---|---|---|
| Etonogestrel implant (Implanon NXT) | about 0.05% | 3 years |
| Levonorgestrel IUD 52 mg (Mirena) | about 0.2% | 5 years or longer for contraception (up to 8 years per current labelling); 5 years when used as the progestogen in MHT |
| Levonorgestrel IUD 19.5 mg (Kyleena) | under 1% | 5 years |
| Copper IUD | about 0.8% | 5 or 10 years depending on device |
| Vasectomy / tubal occlusion | under 0.5% | Permanent |
| DMPA injection (Depo-Provera) | about 4-6% | Every 12 weeks |
| Combined pill, vaginal ring, progestogen-only pill | about 7-9% | Daily (ring monthly) |
| Male condom | about 13% | Also protects against STIs |
| Fertility awareness, withdrawal | about 20% or more | |

**Mechanisms that matter clinically:**
- **Combined hormonal contraception (CHC)** (pill or ring): oestrogen plus progestogen suppress ovulation.
- **Implant and DMPA:** suppress ovulation. Unpredictable bleeding is the main reason for implant removal. DMPA can delay return of fertility by up to about a year and causes reversible bone density loss.
- **LNG-IUD:** thickens cervical mucus and thins the endometrium; many women become lighter or amenorrhoeic.
- **Copper IUD:** copper ions are toxic to sperm and ova and cause an endometrial inflammatory reaction; hormone-free; periods may be heavier and more painful.
- **Progestogen-only pill (POP):** traditional levonorgestrel or norethisterone POPs mainly thicken mucus and must be taken within a **3-hour** window; the **drospirenone POP** inhibits ovulation and has a **24-hour** window.

sections.heading: UKMEC: who can have oestrogen?
sections.body:
UKMEC grades each method for each condition:
| Category | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 1 | No restriction |
| 2 | Benefits generally outweigh risks |
| 3 | Risks generally outweigh benefits; use only with specialist advice when nothing else is acceptable |
| 4 | **Unacceptable health risk: do not use** |

Oestrogen raises the risk of **VTE, stroke and MI**, so most UKMEC 4 conditions apply to CHC. Know these **UKMEC 4 for CHC** examples:
- **Migraine with aura** (at any age) because of ischaemic stroke risk.
- Current or past **VTE**, or a known thrombogenic mutation (e.g. factor V Leiden).
- **Smoker aged 35 or over** smoking **15 or more cigarettes a day**.
- **BP 160/100 mmHg or higher**, or hypertension with vascular disease.
- Ischaemic heart disease, stroke, complicated valvular heart disease.
- **Current breast cancer**.
- Breastfeeding and less than 6 weeks postpartum; major surgery with prolonged immobilisation.
- Systemic lupus with positive antiphospholipid antibodies; severe decompensated cirrhosis or liver tumours.

UKMEC 3 examples: BMI 35 or more; smoker 35 or over with fewer than 15 cigarettes a day; controlled hypertension; multiple cardiovascular risk factors.

**Progestogen-only methods and copper IUDs are safe (UKMEC 1-2) for most of these women**, which is why the implant or an IUD is usually the answer when oestrogen is contraindicated. Exceptions: current breast cancer is UKMEC 4 for all hormonal methods (copper IUD is the choice), and unexplained vaginal bleeding or current PID/STI restrict IUD insertion.

sections.heading: The consultation and young people
sections.body:
**Contraceptive history:** age, pregnancy intention and timing, previous methods and experiences, menstrual problems (a method may treat HMB or dysmenorrhoea), **migraine type**, smoking, BP, BMI, VTE history (personal and family), breastfeeding, medical conditions, **enzyme-inducing drugs**, STI risk, and preferences about bleeding and hormones. Always ask about the possibility of current pregnancy. Check BP and BMI before starting CHC.

**Excluding pregnancy before starting:** a method can be started any time ("quick start") if you are reasonably certain she is not pregnant (e.g. no unprotected sex since last period, within 7 days of a period, correctly using another method). If unsure, quick-start the method with a pregnancy test in 3-4 weeks.

**Young people and consent:**
- Under Australian common law (**Gillick competence**, adopted in *Marion's case*), a person under 18 can consent to medical treatment, including contraception, if they have sufficient maturity and understanding of the nature, risks and consequences. Assess and document it.
- See the young person alone for part of the consultation (a **HEADSS** psychosocial assessment) and explain confidentiality and its limits: serious risk of harm, abuse, or legal requirements.
- **Age of consent** to sex is 16 in most states and 17 in some (e.g. SA and Tasmania); laws on sexual activity between young people close in age, and **mandatory reporting** of child abuse, **vary by state**. A pregnant or sexually active child of 12 or 13, a large age gap, coercion or exploitation should trigger child protection action.
- A young person aged 15 or over can have their own Medicare card.
- Offer STI testing and condoms alongside any method ("dual protection").

sections.heading: How the AMC asks it
sections.body:
- "Most effective reversible method": the **implant**.
- Migraine with aura on the pill: **stop CHC**; offer implant, IUD or POP.
- A 36-year-old smoker of 20 a day wanting the pill: UKMEC 4, offer LARC.
- A 15-year-old alone requesting contraception who understands the risks: Gillick competent, provide it confidentially, but screen for abuse or coercion.
- Breast cancer: copper IUD.

keyPoints: LARCs (implant, LNG-IUD, copper IUD) are the most effective reversible methods and are offered first line to all, including teenagers.
Typical-use failure of the pill is about 7-9%; the implant is about 0.05%.
Australia uses UKMEC; category 4 means do not use.
Migraine with aura, VTE history, smoker 35+ of 15+/day, BP 160/100+ and current breast cancer are UKMEC 4 for combined methods.
Progestogen-only methods and copper IUDs are safe for most women who cannot have oestrogen.
Traditional POP has a 3-hour window; the drospirenone POP has 24 hours.
A Gillick-competent minor can consent to contraception confidentially; screen for abuse and know state reporting laws.
redFlags: Sexual activity in a child under 13, or signs of coercion or exploitation (child protection)
New migraine with aura, severe headache or focal neurology on CHC
Calf pain, chest pain or breathlessness on CHC (VTE)
Possible pregnancy with pelvic pain (exclude ectopic)

contrast.india: Female sterilisation, condoms, copper IUD, DMPA and centchroman (ormeloxifene).
contrast.australia: Implant and hormonal IUD are promoted first line; centchroman is not available.

contrast.india: WHO MEC is the usual reference.
contrast.australia: Australia uses the UK Medical Eligibility Criteria (UKMEC), with near-identical categories 1-4.
Gillick-competent young people can consent confidentially; mandatory reporting rules vary by state.

flashcards.front: Most effective reversible contraceptive?
flashcards.back: Etonogestrel implant (about 0.05% failure), lasts 3 years.

flashcards.front: UKMEC 4 means?
flashcards.back: Unacceptable health risk: the method should not be used.

flashcards.front: Is migraine with aura a contraindication to the combined pill?
flashcards.back: Yes: UKMEC 4 at any age (stroke risk).

flashcards.front: Missed-pill window for a traditional progestogen-only pill?
flashcards.back: 3 hours (drospirenone POP: 24 hours).

flashcards.front: Legal test for a minor's capacity to consent in Australia?
flashcards.back: Gillick competence (endorsed in Marion's case).

flashcards.front: Contraceptive of choice in a woman with current breast cancer?
flashcards.back: Copper IUD (all hormonal methods UKMEC 4).

quiz.stem:
A 23-year-old woman attends a Perth GP clinic requesting the combined oral contraceptive pill. She has migraines about twice a month, preceded by 20 minutes of zigzag lines in her vision. She does not smoke. BP 116/70 mmHg, BMI 23 kg/m2.

What is the most appropriate advice?
options: The combined pill is suitable if she takes it continuously
The combined pill is contraindicated; offer an implant or IUD
She should use a low-dose (20 microgram) combined pill
Start the combined vaginal ring instead of the pill
The combined pill is suitable because she is under 35
quiz.explanation:
Visual zigzags preceding headache describe **migraine with aura**. Under the UKMEC this is **category 4 for all combined hormonal contraception at any age**, because oestrogen adds to the already increased risk of ischaemic stroke in migraine with aura.

Progestogen-only methods and the copper IUD are safe (UKMEC 1-2 for initiation). Offer **LARC** first line (implant or IUD) as the most effective option; the POP is an alternative.
whyWrong: Continuous dosing does not remove the oestrogen-related stroke risk.
Lower oestrogen doses are still UKMEC 4 in migraine with aura.
The ring contains oestrogen and carries the same contraindication.
Age does not change the contraindication for migraine with aura.
quiz.ausPearl: Australian prescribers use the UK Medical Eligibility Criteria (UKMEC) for contraceptive safety.

quiz.stem:
A 15-year-old girl attends a Sydney general practice alone requesting contraception. She has had a 16-year-old boyfriend for 6 months and they have started having sex using condoms. She does not want her parents told. During the consultation she clearly explains how different methods work, their risks and side effects, and why she wants a reliable method.

What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Decline to prescribe until a parent consents
Inform her parents because she is under 16
Prescribe only condoms until she turns 16
Report the relationship to police as statutory rape
Assess and document her competence, then provide contraception confidentially
quiz.explanation:
A person under 18 can consent to treatment if they are **Gillick competent**: mature enough to understand the nature, benefits, risks and consequences. She demonstrates this, so she can consent to contraception, and her confidentiality should be respected. Document your assessment, take a HEADSS history seen alone, screen for coercion or abuse, and offer STI testing and LARC, with condoms for STI protection.

A consensual relationship with a partner close in age is generally not a reportable abuse situation, though laws vary by state; a large age gap, coercion or a child under about 13 would change this.
whyWrong: Parental consent is not needed for a Gillick-competent minor.
Breaching confidentiality without a risk of serious harm damages trust and is not required.
Withholding effective contraception increases her risk of unintended pregnancy.
A consensual relationship with a similar-aged peer is not an automatic police matter; laws vary by state.
quiz.ausPearl: Gillick competence was endorsed by the High Court of Australia in Marion's case (1992). Mandatory reporting obligations vary by state and territory.

quiz.stem:
A 37-year-old woman who smokes 20 cigarettes a day asks to restart the combined oral contraceptive pill she used in her twenties. She has two children and wants no more for now. BP 132/84 mmHg, BMI 29 kg/m2. She has heavy, painful periods.

Which contraceptive is most appropriate to recommend?
options: Combined oral contraceptive pill with smoking cessation advice
Levonorgestrel 52 mg IUD
Copper IUD
Combined vaginal ring
Condoms alone
quiz.explanation:
A smoker **aged 35 or over smoking 15 or more cigarettes a day** is **UKMEC 4** for combined hormonal contraception because of the high risk of MI and stroke. The pill and ring are both combined methods. Of the safe options, the **levonorgestrel 52 mg IUD** also treats her **heavy, painful periods** and is among the most effective methods.

The copper IUD is safe but tends to make periods heavier and more painful. Offer smoking cessation support regardless.
whyWrong: CHC is UKMEC 4 for smokers 35+ of 15 or more a day, whatever advice is given.
Safe, but likely to worsen her heavy, painful periods.
The ring is a combined method with the same contraindication.
Condoms have high typical-use failure and do not treat her bleeding.

lessons.title: Using hormonal methods: pills, LARC and drug interactions
objectives: Manage missed combined pills and know when emergency contraception is needed
Counsel on LARC insertion, side effects and duration
Identify enzyme-inducing drugs and choose an unaffected method
Choose contraception after childbirth, around 40-plus and when bleeding is a problem

sections.heading: From prescription to real life
sections.body: Most contraceptive failures are not about the wrong method but about using the right method imperfectly, drug interactions, or side effects leading to discontinuation. The AMC tests the practical rules: missed pills, interactions, bleeding problems on the implant, and what to use postpartum or near menopause.

sections.heading: Combined pill and ring rules
sections.body:
**Starting:** on day 1-5 of the cycle there is immediate protection; started at any other time (quick start), use condoms or abstain for **7 days**.

**Missed pill rules (for a standard combined pill):** a pill is "missed" when it is **more than 24 hours late** (i.e. more than 48 hours since the last pill was taken).
- **One missed pill:** take it as soon as remembered (even if two pills in one day), continue as usual; no extra precautions.
- **Two or more missed pills:** take the most recent missed pill, continue, and use condoms or abstain for **7 days** (the **7-day rule**, since 7 consecutive active pills restore ovarian suppression).
  - If missed in the **first week** after the hormone-free interval and unprotected sex occurred in that interval or week 1: **emergency contraception**.
  - If missed in the **last week of active pills**: skip the hormone-free (placebo) days and start the next pack straight away.
- Vomiting within about 3 hours or severe diarrhoea counts as a missed pill.

**Non-contraceptive benefits of CHC:** lighter, regular, less painful periods; can be run continuously; improves acne and PCOS symptoms; reduces ovarian and endometrial cancer risk. **Risks:** VTE (small absolute risk, higher with some progestogens such as drospirenone or cyproterone compared with levonorgestrel), stroke, a small increase in breast and cervical cancer risk during use. Common early side effects (breakthrough bleeding, nausea, breast tenderness) often settle within 3 months.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting side effects
sections.body:
| Problem | Approach |
|---|---|
| Breakthrough bleeding on the pill | Check adherence, vomiting, interacting drugs, smoking, STI (chlamydia), pregnancy and cervical screening status; if persistent beyond 3 months, change the progestogen or oestrogen dose |
| Mood change | Take it seriously; try another formulation or a non-hormonal or local (IUD) method |
| Acne on progestogen-only methods | Consider a combined pill with an anti-androgenic progestogen if eligible |
| Amenorrhoea on the pill or LNG-IUD | Exclude pregnancy once; then reassure that it is harmless |
| Heavy periods on the copper IUD | NSAIDs or tranexamic acid during periods; consider switching to the LNG-IUD |
| Weight gain | Evidence of weight gain is consistent only for DMPA |

Always re-check BP and migraine status at each pill review, typically yearly after the first review.

sections.heading: LARC in practice
sections.body:
**Implant (etonogestrel 68 mg rod, Implanon NXT):** inserted subdermally in the inner upper non-dominant arm under local anaesthetic; lasts **3 years**; fertility returns quickly after removal. Main issue: **unpredictable bleeding** (about 1 in 5 women have frequent or prolonged bleeding). Management of troublesome bleeding: exclude pregnancy and STI, check cervical screening status, then a short course of the combined pill (if eligible) or an NSAID can help.

**IUDs:** inserted by trained GPs or gynaecologists. Screen for chlamydia and gonorrhoea (do not delay insertion for asymptomatic women if results can be followed). Risks: **pain and vasovagal reaction** at insertion, **perforation** (about 1-2 per 1000, higher when breastfeeding or postpartum), **expulsion** (about 1 in 20, higher postpartum), infection in the **first 3 weeks** after insertion. If pregnancy occurs with an IUD in place, exclude **ectopic pregnancy**. Teach string checks. "Lost strings": exclude pregnancy, use backup contraception, and arrange **ultrasound** to locate the device (then X-ray if not seen in the uterus, to look for perforation).

**DMPA (medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg IM every 12 weeks):** useful when daily adherence is hard; weight gain in some; **delayed return of fertility**; reversible loss of bone density, so use with caution in adolescents and reassess every couple of years.

sections.heading: Interactions and special situations
sections.body:
**Enzyme-inducing drugs** increase hepatic metabolism of oestrogen and progestogen, reducing the effectiveness of the **combined pill, ring, POP and implant**, and oral emergency contraception:
- Anticonvulsants: **carbamazepine**, phenytoin, phenobarbital, primidone, oxcarbazepine, topiramate (higher doses).
- Antimicrobials: **rifampicin** and rifabutin; some HIV antiretrovirals (e.g. efavirenz, ritonavir-boosted regimens).
- **St John's wort**; modafinil.
- Effects persist for **28 days** after stopping the inducer.
**Unaffected methods:** copper IUD, LNG-IUD and DMPA. Standard antibiotics (e.g. amoxicillin, doxycycline) do **not** reduce CHC effectiveness. Note the reverse interaction: oestrogen lowers **lamotrigine** levels, risking seizures.

**Postpartum:**
- No contraception needed before day 21. Ovulation can occur from about 3-4 weeks in women not breastfeeding.
- Progestogen-only methods (implant, POP, DMPA) are safe any time, including breastfeeding.
- IUDs: within 48 hours of birth, or from **4 weeks** postpartum.
- CHC: **not before 6 weeks if breastfeeding** (UKMEC 4 under 6 weeks); from 3 weeks if not breastfeeding and no other VTE risk factors.
- **Lactational amenorrhoea method** is about 98% effective only if fully breastfeeding, amenorrhoeic and less than 6 months postpartum.

**Women over 40:** fertility is lower but not zero. CHC can continue to 50 in healthy non-smokers without risk factors; progestogen-only methods and IUDs to 55. The LNG-IUD also provides the progestogen for MHT. Stop contraception after 12 months of amenorrhoea if over 50 (24 months if under 50).

**Permanent methods:** vasectomy (simple, local anaesthetic, not immediately effective: backup until **semen analysis confirms azoospermia**, usually around 3 months) and laparoscopic tubal occlusion or salpingectomy (salpingectomy also reduces ovarian cancer risk). LARCs are as effective and reversible, so counsel on regret, especially in younger women.

sections.heading: How the AMC asks it
sections.body:
- Starting carbamazepine or rifampicin on the pill or implant: switch to an **IUD or DMPA**.
- Two pills missed in week 1 with unprotected sex over the pill-free week: **emergency contraception** plus the 7-day rule.
- Pills missed in week 3: **omit the pill-free interval**.
- Frequent bleeding on the implant: exclude pregnancy and STI, check cervical screening, then trial the COC if eligible.
- Breastfeeding at 4 weeks: implant or POP, not CHC.
- Vasectomy: not effective until azoospermia is confirmed.

keyPoints: A combined pill is missed when more than 24 hours late; two or more missed triggers the 7-day rule.
Missed pills in week 1 plus unprotected sex: emergency contraception. In week 3: skip the pill-free days.
Enzyme inducers (carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampicin, St John's wort) reduce pill, ring, POP and implant effectiveness; use IUD or DMPA.
Ordinary antibiotics do not reduce pill effectiveness.
Implant: 3 years; unpredictable bleeding is the commonest reason for removal.
Breastfeeding under 6 weeks postpartum is UKMEC 4 for combined methods; progestogen-only methods are safe.
Vasectomy needs backup until a semen analysis shows azoospermia.
redFlags: Positive pregnancy test with an IUD in situ (exclude ectopic)
Fever and pelvic pain within 3 weeks of IUD insertion (PID)
Unilateral leg swelling or chest pain on CHC

contrast.india: DMPA is widely used, including by adolescents, through public programs.
contrast.australia: Available but used with caution in adolescents because of bone density; LARC is preferred.

contrast.india: Interactions with anti-TB and anti-epileptic drugs are common in practice given high TB prevalence.
contrast.australia: Same principle; rifampicin and anticonvulsant interactions are tested, and IUD or DMPA is the recommended alternative.

flashcards.front: When is a combined pill counted as missed?
flashcards.back: More than 24 hours late (48+ hours since the last pill).

flashcards.front: What is the 7-day rule?
flashcards.back: After 2+ missed pills, use condoms or abstain until 7 consecutive active pills are taken.

flashcards.front: Contraceptive methods unaffected by enzyme inducers?
flashcards.back: Copper IUD, LNG-IUD and DMPA.

flashcards.front: How long do enzyme-inducer effects persist after stopping?
flashcards.back: About 28 days.

flashcards.front: Earliest a breastfeeding woman can start the combined pill?
flashcards.back: 6 weeks postpartum.

flashcards.front: When is a vasectomy considered effective?
flashcards.back: After semen analysis confirms azoospermia (usually around 3 months).

quiz.stem:
A 26-year-old woman using the combined oral contraceptive pill (21 active, 7 placebo) calls her GP. She forgot to start her new pack and has now missed the first 2 active pills (it is day 3 of the new pack). She had unprotected sex 2 days ago.

What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Take one pill now and continue; no further action needed
Take the most recent missed pill, continue the pack and skip the next placebo week
Stop this pack and restart a new pack after her next period
Take the most recent missed pill, continue the pack, use condoms for 7 days, and take emergency contraception
Double the dose of pills for the rest of the week
quiz.explanation:
Missing pills at the **start of a pack** extends the hormone-free interval, the most dangerous time, because ovulation can escape suppression. With **two or more** pills missed in **week 1** and **unprotected sex** in the pill-free interval or week 1, she needs **emergency contraception** as well as the **7-day rule** (take the latest missed pill, continue, and use condoms or abstain until she has taken 7 consecutive active pills).

Skipping the placebo week applies when pills are missed in the last week of the pack.
whyWrong: Ignores the risk from unprotected sex during an extended hormone-free interval.
Skipping placebos is for pills missed in week 3, and emergency contraception is still needed here.
Stopping leaves her unprotected and does not address the recent unprotected sex.
Extra pills do not restore protection and increase side effects.

quiz.stem:
A 29-year-old woman with epilepsy has been using an etonogestrel implant for 1 year. Her neurologist has just started carbamazepine because her previous medication was not controlling seizures. She wants to avoid pregnancy for at least 3 years.

What is the most appropriate contraceptive advice?
options: Change to a levonorgestrel IUD
Replace the implant with the combined pill at a standard dose
Continue the implant; carbamazepine does not affect it
Add the progestogen-only pill to the implant
Replace the implant every 12 months instead of every 3 years
quiz.explanation:
**Carbamazepine is a potent enzyme inducer**. It increases metabolism of etonogestrel and so reduces implant effectiveness, and similarly affects the combined pill, ring and POP. Methods **unaffected by enzyme inducers** are the **LNG-IUD, copper IUD and DMPA**. The LNG-IUD acts locally in the uterus, so its contraceptive effect does not depend on systemic hormone levels.

The effect of enzyme inducers persists for about 28 days after stopping them, so interim condoms are advised until the IUD is in place. Also consider pre-pregnancy counselling and folic acid given antiepileptic teratogenicity.
whyWrong: The combined pill is also affected by enzyme induction.
Enzyme induction reduces implant effectiveness.
The POP is equally affected; adding it does not restore reliability.
More frequent replacement does not overcome enzyme induction.

quiz.stem:
A 30-year-old woman who is fully breastfeeding her 4-week-old baby asks about contraception. She had a vaginal birth. She would like something she does not have to remember daily and plans another child in about 2 years.

Which method is most appropriate to offer now?
options: Combined oral contraceptive pill
Combined vaginal ring
Lactational amenorrhoea method for 12 months
Tubal ligation
Etonogestrel implant
quiz.explanation:
In a woman **breastfeeding and under 6 weeks postpartum**, combined hormonal methods are **UKMEC 4** (VTE risk and possible effect on milk supply). **Progestogen-only methods are safe at any time postpartum**, including while breastfeeding. The **implant** needs no daily action, is highly effective, and fertility returns promptly on removal, suiting her plan for another child in 2 years.

The lactational amenorrhoea method is only reliable while fully breastfeeding, amenorrhoeic and less than 6 months postpartum.
whyWrong: UKMEC 4 when breastfeeding under 6 weeks postpartum.
The ring contains oestrogen and has the same restriction.
LAM is reliable only up to 6 months postpartum and while strict criteria are met.
Permanent sterilisation does not fit her plan for another child.

lessons.title: Emergency contraception
objectives: Choose between the copper IUD, ulipristal and levonorgestrel emergency contraception
Apply the time limits and factors that reduce oral EC effectiveness
Start ongoing contraception safely after emergency contraception
Arrange follow-up pregnancy testing and STI screening

sections.heading: What it is and why it matters
sections.body: Emergency contraception (EC) reduces the chance of pregnancy after unprotected sex, contraceptive failure (broken condom, missed pills) or sexual assault. In Australia, both oral options are available **from pharmacies without a prescription**, and the copper IUD can be inserted by trained GPs or at sexual health and family planning clinics. The AMC tests which method to pick given timing, weight, drugs and breastfeeding, and what to do next.

sections.heading: The three options
sections.body:
| Method | Time limit after unprotected sex | Mechanism | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Copper IUD** | Up to **5 days** (120 hours), or up to 5 days after the earliest expected ovulation | Toxic to sperm and ova; prevents implantation | **Most effective** (failure under 0.1%); provides ongoing contraception; unaffected by weight or drugs |
| **Ulipristal acetate 30 mg** (single oral dose) | Up to **120 hours** | Selective progesterone receptor modulator; delays ovulation even after the LH surge has begun | More effective than levonorgestrel; pharmacy availability |
| **Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg** (single oral dose) | Licensed to **72 hours**; effectiveness falls with time | Delays ovulation, but not once the LH surge has started | Pharmacy availability |

Oral methods **do not** work after ovulation has occurred and do not disrupt an established pregnancy; they are not abortifacients. Neither protects against further unprotected sex later in the same cycle, so ongoing contraception is essential.

**Factors that reduce oral EC effectiveness:**
- **Enzyme inducers:** use the copper IUD, or a **double dose of levonorgestrel (3 mg)**; ulipristal is not recommended.
- **Higher body weight:** levonorgestrel is less effective at higher BMI or weight; guidance suggests the copper IUD first, or ulipristal, or a double dose of levonorgestrel (check the current Australian or UK guidance for exact thresholds).
- **Recent progestogen use:** progestogen taken in the 7 days before ulipristal may reduce its effect.

sections.heading: Assessing the need for EC
sections.body:
Take a brief, focused history:
- **Date of the last menstrual period** and usual cycle length, to estimate where she is in the cycle. The fertile window is roughly the 5 days before ovulation and the day of ovulation; sperm can survive up to 5 days.
- **Every episode of unprotected sex since the last period**, not just the most recent one. If there was an earlier episode more than 5 days ago, she may already be pregnant: do a pregnancy test (it may be too early to be positive) and still give EC for the recent episode, with a repeat test in 3 weeks.
- **Current contraception and how it failed:** missed pills, late DMPA injection (more than 14 weeks since the last), expired implant, expelled IUD, condom failure.
- **Medicines** (enzyme inducers), **weight**, breastfeeding, and whether she has already used ulipristal or levonorgestrel this cycle.
- **Safety:** consent, coercion, age and partner age, sexual assault.

Reassure her that oral EC is **not harmful if she turns out to be already pregnant**: there is no evidence of teratogenicity, and it will not end an established pregnancy. EC is safe for virtually all women, including those for whom oestrogen is contraindicated (UKMEC 1), so there are no medical reasons to withhold oral EC.

The copper IUD has the usual IUD contraindications (current pregnancy, untreated PID or STI with symptoms, unexplained bleeding, distorted cavity), and an STI test should be taken at insertion; prophylactic antibiotics may be considered if risk is high and results are pending.

sections.heading: After EC: starting contraception and follow-up
sections.body:
**Ongoing contraception:**
- **After levonorgestrel:** start (quick start) hormonal contraception **immediately**, with condoms or abstinence for 7 days (2 days for POP).
- **After ulipristal:** **wait 5 days** before starting hormonal contraception, because progestogen can block ulipristal's effect on ovulation. Use condoms or abstain meanwhile and for the method's usual extra days after starting.
- **Copper IUD** provides immediate ongoing contraception; it can be kept long term or removed after the next period once another method is in place.

**Breastfeeding:** levonorgestrel is compatible; after ulipristal, the manufacturer advises expressing and discarding breast milk for a week.

**Follow-up:**
- **Pregnancy test in 3 weeks** if the next period is more than 7 days late, lighter than usual, or abnormal.
- Offer **STI testing** (chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT; HIV and syphilis serology when indicated).
- After **sexual assault**, EC is one part of care: consider HIV PEP (within 72 hours), STI prophylaxis, hepatitis B vaccination, forensic examination through a specialist sexual assault service, and psychological support; respect her choices about police involvement.
- Repeated EC use in a cycle is allowed (repeat the same drug; don't mix levonorgestrel and ulipristal within 5 days), but it signals the need for a reliable ongoing method, ideally LARC.

sections.heading: Choosing in common scenarios
sections.body:
| Scenario | Best choice |
|---|---|
| Unprotected sex 4 days ago, wants the most effective option | Copper IUD |
| 90 hours ago, IUD not acceptable | Ulipristal |
| 24 hours ago, taking carbamazepine, IUD declined | Levonorgestrel 3 mg (double dose) |
| Breastfeeding, 30 hours ago, IUD declined | Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg |
| Wants to start the pill today, 48 hours ago, IUD declined | Levonorgestrel (so the pill can start immediately), or ulipristal and wait 5 days before starting |
| Already ovulated and unprotected sex 3 days ago | Copper IUD (oral methods won't work after ovulation) |

For **young people**, a Gillick-competent minor can obtain EC; a pharmacist or doctor should still consider safeguarding (age, partner age, coercion).

sections.heading: How the AMC asks it
sections.body:
- "Most effective emergency contraception" is **copper IUD** (within 5 days).
- 72-120 hours and no IUD: **ulipristal**.
- Enzyme inducer: copper IUD or **levonorgestrel 3 mg**; not ulipristal.
- After ulipristal: **wait 5 days** before hormonal contraception.
- Always arrange a pregnancy test if the period is late and offer STI screening.

keyPoints: Copper IUD within 5 days is the most effective EC and provides ongoing contraception.
Ulipristal 30 mg works up to 120 hours; levonorgestrel 1.5 mg is best within 72 hours.
Both oral EC drugs are available from Australian pharmacies without prescription.
Enzyme inducers: copper IUD or double-dose levonorgestrel (3 mg); avoid ulipristal.
After ulipristal, wait 5 days before starting hormonal contraception.
Pregnancy test if the period is more than 7 days late; offer STI testing.
redFlags: Sexual assault (PEP, forensic and psychological care)
Young age, large partner age gap or coercion (child protection)
Abdominal pain or abnormal bleeding after EC (exclude ectopic pregnancy)

contrast.india: Levonorgestrel EC is sold over the counter; ulipristal is less widely available.
contrast.australia: Both levonorgestrel and ulipristal are available from pharmacies without a prescription.
Recommended as the most effective EC and offered through GPs trained in insertion and sexual health or family planning clinics.

flashcards.front: Most effective emergency contraceptive?
flashcards.back: Copper IUD, within 5 days (120 hours).

flashcards.front: Time limit for ulipristal acetate 30 mg?
flashcards.back: Up to 120 hours after unprotected sex.

flashcards.front: Levonorgestrel EC dose for a woman on an enzyme inducer?
flashcards.back: 3 mg (double dose), or a copper IUD.

flashcards.front: How long to wait after ulipristal before starting hormonal contraception?
flashcards.back: 5 days.

flashcards.front: When to check a pregnancy test after oral EC?
flashcards.back: If the period is more than 7 days late or abnormal (about 3 weeks after EC).

quiz.stem:
A 21-year-old woman presents to a GP clinic 100 hours after a condom broke during intercourse. She is on no contraception. Her last period started 12 days ago; cycles are regular at 28 days. She declines an IUD insertion.

Which is the most appropriate emergency contraception?
options: Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg orally
Levonorgestrel 3 mg orally
Ulipristal acetate 30 mg orally
Combined oral contraceptive pills taken as a double dose
No emergency contraception is effective after 72 hours
quiz.explanation:
At **100 hours**, levonorgestrel is outside its licensed window (72 hours) and less effective. **Ulipristal acetate** is licensed up to **120 hours** and delays ovulation even after the LH surge has started, making it more effective than levonorgestrel, particularly around ovulation (she is on day 12).

The copper IUD would be the most effective choice but she declined it. After ulipristal she should wait 5 days before starting hormonal contraception, and have a pregnancy test if her period is late.
whyWrong: Beyond its 72-hour window and less effective near ovulation.
A double dose is for enzyme inducers, not late presentation.
The old Yuzpe method is less effective and not recommended.
Ulipristal and the copper IUD work up to 120 hours.
quiz.ausPearl: Both ulipristal and levonorgestrel emergency contraception are available from Australian pharmacies without a prescription.

quiz.stem:
A 25-year-old woman had unprotected intercourse 30 hours ago. She takes carbamazepine for epilepsy. She is anxious about procedures and declines an IUD.

What is the most appropriate emergency contraception?
options: Ulipristal acetate 30 mg
Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg
Levonorgestrel 3 mg
Ulipristal acetate 60 mg
Mifepristone 200 mg
quiz.explanation:
**Carbamazepine induces liver enzymes**, reducing levels of both oral EC drugs. The **copper IUD** is unaffected and best, but she declined. The recommended oral alternative is a **double dose of levonorgestrel (3 mg)** as soon as possible.

Ulipristal is **not recommended** with enzyme inducers, and doubling it is not an established regimen. Mifepristone is an abortifacient, not an emergency contraceptive in Australia. She should also be counselled about a reliable ongoing method unaffected by her medicine, such as an IUD or DMPA.
whyWrong: Ulipristal is not recommended with enzyme inducers.
A standard dose is likely to be inadequate with carbamazepine.
Doubling ulipristal is not an established or recommended regimen.
Mifepristone is used for medical abortion, not as EC in Australia.

quiz.stem:
A 19-year-old woman takes ulipristal acetate 30 mg emergency contraception today after unprotected sex 2 days ago. She wants to start the combined oral contraceptive pill as soon as possible. She has no contraindications.

What is the most appropriate advice about starting the pill?
options: Wait 5 days, then start the pill and use condoms for the next 7 days
Start the pill today and use condoms for 7 days
Wait until her next period before starting
Start the pill today with no extra precautions
Wait 21 days and do a pregnancy test before starting
quiz.explanation:
Progestogens taken soon after ulipristal can **counteract its ovulation-delaying action**, reducing EC effectiveness. Guidance is therefore to **wait 5 days** after ulipristal before starting hormonal contraception, using condoms or abstaining meanwhile, then follow the method's usual extra precautions (7 days for the combined pill).

She should also do a pregnancy test if her next period is more than 7 days late or abnormal. If she had taken levonorgestrel instead, she could quick-start the pill immediately.
whyWrong: The problem is interaction with ulipristal, not only backup cover.
Waiting for a period needlessly delays effective contraception.
Starting now risks reducing ulipristal effectiveness.
Waiting 3 weeks is unnecessary; she can quick-start after 5 days.

lessons.title: Abortion: law, medical and surgical care
objectives: Explain how abortion is regulated in Australia and the duties of a conscientious objector
Assess a woman requesting termination, including dating and excluding ectopic pregnancy
Describe the medical abortion regimen, its contraindications and follow-up
Recognise complications after abortion

sections.heading: Law and access in Australia
sections.body:
Abortion is **legal in every Australian state and territory** and is regulated by **state or territory law**, not a national Act (unlike India's Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act). Over the past decade all jurisdictions have removed abortion from their criminal codes and treat it as health care. The details **vary by jurisdiction**:
- **Gestational limits** for abortion on request differ (roughly 16 to 24 weeks depending on the state), after which additional requirements usually apply, typically the agreement of two medical practitioners.
- **Safe access zones** around clinics prohibit harassment of patients and staff in most jurisdictions.
- **Conscientious objection:** a doctor may decline to participate, but in most jurisdictions must **disclose the objection and refer** the patient, or give information on where to obtain care, without delay. The objection does **not** apply in an emergency where abortion is needed to save the woman's life.

Early medical abortion is available through general practice and telehealth, and in 2023 the TGA removed the requirement for special prescriber certification and pharmacy registration, making access much easier (including prescribing by nurse practitioners). Cost and distance remain barriers in rural areas. A young person who is Gillick competent can consent to abortion.

sections.heading: Assessment before abortion
sections.body:
- **Confirm pregnancy and gestation:** from LMP, with **ultrasound** where indicated (uncertain dates, pain or bleeding, risk factors for ectopic). Ultrasound is not mandatory in every case in current Australian practice when history and examination are reliable, but **ectopic pregnancy must be actively excluded**.
- **Decision-making:** is she certain, is she making the decision freely (screen for reproductive coercion and family violence), does she want counselling (optional, not mandatory)?
- **Medical history:** bleeding disorders, anticoagulants, long-term corticosteroids, adrenal insufficiency, porphyria, severe asthma, IUD in situ, allergies.
- **Blood tests** as indicated: Hb, blood group and Rh D status (practice on anti-D for early medical abortion has changed; follow current local and RANZCOG guidance), quantitative hCG as a baseline.
- **STI screen** (chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT), and cervical screening if due.
- **Contraception plan** before she leaves: ovulation can return within about 2 weeks.

sections.heading: Medical and surgical abortion
sections.body:
**Early medical abortion (up to 63 days, 9 weeks gestation):**
- **Mifepristone 200 mg orally** (a progesterone receptor antagonist: the decidua breaks down and the cervix softens), then **24-48 hours later misoprostol 800 microgram buccally** (a prostaglandin E1 analogue: uterine contractions expel the pregnancy). In Australia these are supplied together as a composite pack.
- Expect cramping and bleeding heavier than a period for several hours, then lighter bleeding for up to 2 weeks or so. Analgesia: NSAIDs and paracetamol.
- **Contraindications:** confirmed or suspected **ectopic pregnancy**, IUD in situ (remove first), chronic adrenal failure, long-term corticosteroid therapy, inherited porphyria, haemorrhagic disorders or anticoagulation, allergy, gestation beyond the approved limit.
- **Confirm success** at follow-up (typically 2-3 weeks): a serum hCG fall of about 80% or more, or a **low-sensitivity urine pregnancy test**, with symptom review. Success is about 95-98%; failure or incomplete abortion is managed with repeat misoprostol or aspiration.
- **Teratogenicity:** misoprostol is teratogenic (limb and cranial nerve defects, Mobius syndrome); if the pregnancy continues, counsel strongly and offer surgical completion.

**Surgical abortion:** **vacuum (suction) aspiration** in the first trimester, often under local anaesthetic with sedation, with cervical priming (misoprostol) beforehand; **dilatation and evacuation** in the second trimester by trained providers. Later medical abortion uses mifepristone and repeated misoprostol with induction of labour.

**Complications:** incomplete abortion (retained products: ongoing bleeding and pain, open os), **infection** (fever, pelvic pain, offensive discharge), haemorrhage, continuing pregnancy, rarely uterine perforation or cervical injury (surgical). Abortion does not increase the risk of future infertility or breast cancer, and does not cause mental illness, though women with prior mental health problems may need support.

sections.heading: Aftercare and follow-up
sections.body:
- **Contraception:** the **implant** or DMPA can be given on the day mifepristone is taken; the pill can start on the day of misoprostol or the next day. An IUD can be inserted immediately after surgical abortion or once medical abortion is confirmed complete.
- **Safety-netting:** seek urgent care for soaking more than 2 large pads an hour for 2 hours, fever or feeling unwell more than 24 hours after misoprostol (sepsis, including rare clostridial infection), severe pain not relieved by analgesia, or no bleeding within 24-48 hours of misoprostol (possible failure or ectopic).
- **Emotional support:** most women feel relief; offer counselling services for those who want them.
- Ensure a clear follow-up pathway, including telehealth services, for rural women.

sections.heading: Medical or surgical: helping her choose
sections.body:
| | Early medical abortion | Surgical (aspiration) |
|---|---|---|
| Gestation | Up to 63 days (MS-2 Step) | First trimester and beyond (D&E later) |
| Setting | Home, after GP or telehealth consult | Clinic or day surgery |
| Procedure | Tablets; bleeding and cramps at home | Brief procedure, local anaesthetic or sedation |
| Success | About 95-98% | About 99% |
| Bleeding | Heavier and longer | Lighter, shorter |
| Visits | Consult plus follow-up test | Usually a single procedure day plus follow-up |
| Contraception | Implant or DMPA on day 1; IUD after completion | IUD can be inserted at the procedure |

Women value privacy and avoiding instruments (medical) or speed and certainty (surgical). Both are safe; both are far safer than continuing a pregnancy to term. Offer the choice where both are available.

sections.heading: How the AMC asks it
sections.body:
- The law is **state-based**: when asked, say "varies by state" and know that objecting doctors must usually **refer on**.
- Before medical abortion, **exclude ectopic pregnancy** (pain or bleeding: ultrasound and hCG).
- Mifepristone then misoprostol **24-48 hours later**, up to **63 days**.
- IUD in situ: remove before medical abortion.
- Fever and prolonged bleeding a week after: incomplete abortion with infection, needing antibiotics and possibly aspiration.

keyPoints: Abortion is legal throughout Australia and regulated by state or territory law; gestational limits vary.
Conscientious objectors must, in most jurisdictions, disclose and refer on, and must help in an emergency.
Early medical abortion: mifepristone 200 mg, then misoprostol 800 microgram buccally 24-48 hours later, up to 63 days.
Exclude ectopic pregnancy before medical abortion.
Contraindications include ectopic, IUD in situ, adrenal failure, long-term steroids, porphyria, bleeding disorders.
Confirm completion with serum hCG or a low-sensitivity urine test at 2-3 weeks.
Start contraception at the time of abortion; the implant can go in on the mifepristone day.
redFlags: Pain or bleeding with an empty uterus on ultrasound (ectopic pregnancy)
Soaking more than 2 pads an hour for 2 hours after misoprostol
Fever, tachycardia or feeling unwell more than 24 hours after misoprostol (sepsis)
No bleeding after misoprostol (failed abortion or ectopic)

contrast.india: National Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act with gestation limits and required medical opinions.
contrast.australia: State and territory law; decriminalised everywhere; limits and requirements vary by jurisdiction.

contrast.india: Provided by registered medical practitioners at approved sites.
contrast.australia: Early medical abortion is prescribed in general practice and by telehealth, by doctors and nurse practitioners, dispensed by community pharmacists.

flashcards.front: Early medical abortion regimen in Australia?
flashcards.back: Mifepristone 200 mg orally, then misoprostol 800 microgram buccally 24-48 hours later.

flashcards.front: Gestational limit for early medical abortion with MS-2 Step?
flashcards.back: 63 days (9 weeks).

flashcards.front: What must be excluded before medical abortion?
flashcards.back: Ectopic pregnancy.

flashcards.front: How is completion of medical abortion confirmed?
flashcards.back: Serum hCG fall (about 80%+) or a low-sensitivity urine pregnancy test at 2-3 weeks.

flashcards.front: Duty of a conscientiously objecting doctor in most states?
flashcards.back: Disclose the objection and refer on, or provide information; must assist in an emergency.

quiz.stem:
A 27-year-old woman in regional Victoria requests an abortion. Her last period was 6 weeks ago and a home pregnancy test is positive. She has had some left-sided pelvic pain and light spotting for 2 days. She is otherwise well, BP 118/74 mmHg, HR 80 bpm. She wants a medical abortion.

What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Prescribe mifepristone and misoprostol today
Prescribe misoprostol alone
Refer for surgical abortion because of the bleeding
Arrange pelvic ultrasound and a quantitative serum hCG
Advise her to wait 2 weeks and repeat the pregnancy test
quiz.explanation:
Before medical abortion, **ectopic pregnancy must be excluded**, and she has **pain and spotting**, both warning features. Mifepristone and misoprostol do not treat an ectopic, and the cramping and bleeding they cause could mask a rupture. She needs a **pelvic ultrasound** (to confirm an intrauterine pregnancy and gestation) and a **quantitative hCG**.

Once an intrauterine pregnancy is confirmed within 63 days, medical abortion can proceed. Surgical abortion is an option, but bleeding alone does not mandate it, and delay is not appropriate.
whyWrong: Prescribing before excluding ectopic pregnancy is unsafe given her symptoms.
Misoprostol alone is less effective and still requires ectopic exclusion.
Bleeding is not a reason to insist on surgery; ectopic exclusion comes first either way.
Delay is unnecessary and potentially dangerous if this is an ectopic.

quiz.stem:
A GP in Brisbane holds a conscientious objection to abortion. A 32-year-old patient, 7 weeks pregnant, asks him for a medical abortion.

According to the law in most Australian jurisdictions, what must the GP do?
options: Prescribe the medication despite his objection
Disclose his objection and refer her to, or tell her how to find, a provider who does not object
Refuse and give no further information
Counsel her to continue the pregnancy
Require her to see a psychiatrist before referral
quiz.explanation:
Doctors may conscientiously object to participating in abortion, but in most Australian jurisdictions (including Queensland) the law requires them to **disclose the objection and refer** the patient to, or give information about, another provider who does not object. The Medical Board of Australia's code of conduct also requires that an objection does not impede access to care, and that patients are not disadvantaged.

The objection does not extend to emergencies where treatment is needed to save a life. Trying to dissuade her, or adding hurdles, breaches professional standards.
whyWrong: He is not obliged to provide it personally if he objects.
Refusing without referral or information breaches the law in most jurisdictions and the professional code.
Imposing his own views is unprofessional and not permitted.
There is no requirement for psychiatric assessment before abortion.
quiz.ausPearl: Abortion law is state-based in Australia; conscientious objection provisions differ in detail but most require referral or information.

quiz.stem:
A 24-year-old woman had an early medical abortion at 7 weeks with mifepristone followed by misoprostol 9 days ago. She now reports ongoing bleeding with clots, lower abdominal pain and an offensive discharge. Temperature 38.3 degrees C, HR 102 bpm, BP 116/72 mmHg. The uterus is tender and the cervical os is open. Ultrasound shows heterogeneous material in the uterine cavity.

What is the most appropriate management?
options: Reassure her that this is normal after medical abortion
Repeat misoprostol alone at home
Oral doxycycline alone and review in a week
Arrange a repeat ultrasound in 2 weeks
Admit for IV antibiotics and uterine aspiration of retained products
quiz.explanation:
Fever, tachycardia, a tender uterus, an open os, offensive discharge and retained material mean **incomplete abortion with infection (septic incomplete abortion)**. This needs **admission, blood cultures, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics** (covering anaerobes, gram-negatives and STI organisms) and **evacuation (aspiration) of retained products** once antibiotics are started.

Delayed treatment risks sepsis. Repeat misoprostol is an option for uncomplicated incomplete abortion, but not with systemic infection.
whyWrong: Fever and offensive discharge are not normal after abortion.
Misoprostol alone does not treat infection and she is systemically unwell.
Oral single-agent therapy is inadequate for a systemically unwell patient with retained tissue.
Delay risks progression to sepsis.

lessons.title: Infertility: initial assessment and treatment
objectives: Know when to start investigating infertility and why both partners are assessed together
Order and interpret the first-line female and male investigations
Give preconception advice that improves outcomes
Outline treatment options from ovulation induction to IVF and when to refer

sections.heading: When and why
sections.body:
**Infertility** is failure to conceive after **12 months** of regular unprotected intercourse. About 1 in 6 Australian couples experience it. Because fertility declines with female age, especially after 35, investigation starts after **6 months if the woman is 35 or older**, and **immediately** if there is a known cause (amenorrhoea, known tubal disease or endometriosis, previous chemotherapy, known male factor).

Causes are roughly shared: **ovulatory** (about a quarter, mostly PCOS), **tubal and pelvic** (PID, endometriosis, previous surgery), **male factor** (about 30-40% contributes), and **unexplained** (about a quarter). Several factors often coexist. Australia has one of the world's highest rates of assisted reproduction use, subsidised through **Medicare**; genital TB, an important cause in India, is rare except in migrants from high-prevalence countries.

sections.heading: Why conception fails
sections.body:
Conception needs: a **good-quality egg released** (ovulation), **sperm** in adequate number and function, **patent tubes** where fertilisation occurs, and a **receptive uterus**.
- **Ovulatory dysfunction:** PCOS (commonest), hypothalamic amenorrhoea, hyperprolactinaemia, thyroid disease, premature ovarian insufficiency, and **age-related decline in egg quantity and quality**.
- **Tubal:** scarring from chlamydia or gonorrhoea PID, pelvic surgery, endometriosis; hydrosalpinx fluid is also toxic to embryos.
- **Uterine:** submucosal fibroids, polyps, Asherman syndrome, congenital anomalies.
- **Male:** idiopathic, varicocele, previous testicular injury or undescended testes, infection, **anabolic steroids or exogenous testosterone** (suppresses spermatogenesis), heat, smoking, obesity, genetic causes (Klinefelter syndrome, Y-chromosome microdeletions, cystic fibrosis with congenital absence of the vas deferens).

sections.heading: History and examination
sections.body:
Take the history **from both partners, ideally together**:
- Duration of trying, frequency and timing of intercourse, sexual dysfunction.
- **Female:** age, cycle length and regularity (regular cycles of 21-35 days suggest ovulation), dysmenorrhoea and dyspareunia (endometriosis), previous STIs or PID, pelvic surgery, previous pregnancies, hirsutism, galactorrhoea, weight changes, medications.
- **Male:** previous paternity, mumps orchitis, undescended testes, testicular surgery, **testosterone or anabolic steroid use**, drugs, heat exposure.
- **Both:** smoking, alcohol, BMI, occupation, chronic illness, family history of genetic conditions.

Examination: BMI, signs of hyperandrogenism or thyroid disease, pelvic examination. Male: testicular volume, varicocele, presence of the vas deferens, secondary sexual characteristics.

sections.heading: First-line tests
sections.body:
**Female:**
- **Confirm ovulation:** **mid-luteal serum progesterone** about 7 days before the expected period (day 21 of a 28-day cycle); a clearly raised level confirms ovulation.
- **TSH, prolactin**; FSH/LH and oestradiol in the early follicular phase if cycles are irregular; testosterone if hyperandrogenic.
- **AMH** estimates ovarian reserve (helps plan IVF and counsel on time available) but does **not** predict natural conception.
- **Pelvic ultrasound** (fibroids, polycystic morphology, endometrioma, hydrosalpinx).
- **Tubal patency:** **HyCoSy** (hysterosalpingo-contrast sonography) or HSG; laparoscopy with dye if endometriosis or tubal disease is suspected.
- **Preconception bloods:** rubella and varicella immunity, blood group and antibodies, HIV, hepatitis B and C, syphilis, FBC; **chlamydia** NAAT; cervical screening up to date. Offer **reproductive carrier screening** (cystic fibrosis, spinal muscular atrophy, fragile X), which is Medicare-funded.

**Male:**
- **Semen analysis** (after 2-7 days' abstinence, assessed against WHO reference values). If abnormal, **repeat** in about 3 months (spermatogenesis takes around 72 days).
- If severely abnormal or azoospermic: FSH, LH, testosterone, karyotype, Y-chromosome microdeletion testing, CFTR genes, and urology/andrology referral.

sections.heading: Reading the results
sections.body:
| Finding | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| Low mid-luteal progesterone, irregular cycles, high LH:FSH, high androgens | PCOS anovulation |
| Low progesterone, low FSH/LH, low oestradiol, low BMI | Hypothalamic anovulation |
| High FSH, low AMH, woman under 40 | Premature ovarian insufficiency |
| Raised prolactin | Medicine-induced or prolactinoma |
| Blocked tubes or hydrosalpinx | Tubal factor (often previous PID) |
| Azoospermia, high FSH, small testes | Testicular failure (e.g. Klinefelter) |
| Azoospermia, low FSH/LH | Hypogonadotrophic, including exogenous testosterone |
| Azoospermia, normal FSH, normal testes | Obstruction (e.g. absent vas in CF gene carriers) |
| All tests normal | Unexplained infertility |

sections.heading: Advice and treatment
sections.body:
**Preconception and lifestyle advice for both partners:**
- Regular intercourse every **2-3 days** throughout the cycle (reduces stress of timed sex).
- **Folic acid** at least 1 month before conception and through the first trimester (0.4-0.5 mg; **5 mg** if higher risk: previous neural tube defect, diabetes, obesity, antiepileptics), and **iodine 150 microgram daily**.
- Stop smoking, reduce alcohol (no alcohol is safest in pregnancy), healthy weight, review medicines (stop exogenous testosterone), update vaccinations (MMR and varicella at least 1 month before conception).

**Treatment by cause (specialist fertility services):**
- **Anovulation:** **letrozole** first line in PCOS (clomiphene alternative), gonadotrophins; weight loss; treat thyroid disease or hyperprolactinaemia (cabergoline).
- **Tubal disease:** IVF (tubal surgery occasionally); remove hydrosalpinges before IVF.
- **Endometriosis:** surgery for some, IVF.
- **Male factor:** correct reversible causes; **ICSI** (intracytoplasmic sperm injection) for severe male factor; surgical sperm retrieval for obstructive azoospermia.
- **Unexplained:** expectant management for a period if young, IUI with ovarian stimulation, or IVF.
- **IVF** risks: **ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome** (abdominal distension, ascites, haemoconcentration, VTE), multiple pregnancy (reduced by single embryo transfer, standard in Australia), and the emotional and financial load. **Donor gametes** and **altruistic surrogacy** are legal (commercial surrogacy is illegal), with rules varying by state; donor-conceived people can usually access donor identity information.

**Refer** to a fertility specialist early when the woman is 35 or older, has known risk factors, or the semen analysis is abnormal. Support the couple's mental health throughout.

sections.heading: How the AMC asks it
sections.body:
- Timing: **12 months**, or **6 months if 35+**; earlier with known risk factors.
- Always assess **both partners**: a semen analysis is part of the first round, not an afterthought.
- Man using testosterone or anabolic steroids with azoospermia: stop it (suppresses FSH/LH).
- Day 21 progesterone confirms ovulation only in a 28-day cycle; time it 7 days before the expected period.
- AMH measures reserve, not fertility.
- Previous PID with regular cycles and normal semen: think **tubal factor**, test patency.

keyPoints: Investigate after 12 months of trying, or 6 months if the woman is 35 or older, or immediately with known risk factors.
Assess both partners together; semen analysis is a first-line test.
Mid-luteal progesterone (7 days before the expected period) confirms ovulation.
HyCoSy or HSG tests tubal patency; laparoscopy if endometriosis or tubal disease is suspected.
AMH estimates ovarian reserve but does not predict natural conception.
Preconception: folic acid (5 mg if high risk), iodine 150 microgram, stop smoking, check immunity, offer carrier screening.
Letrozole for anovulatory PCOS; IVF for tubal disease; ICSI for severe male factor.
redFlags: Azoospermia (genetic, obstructive or testicular causes; urology referral)
Amenorrhoea with high FSH in a young woman (POI)
Abdominal distension, breathlessness and oliguria during IVF (ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)
Positive pregnancy test with pain after fertility treatment (ectopic or heterotopic pregnancy)

contrast.india: Genital tuberculosis is an important cause of tubal infertility.
contrast.australia: Genital TB is rare; tubal factor usually follows chlamydial PID. Consider TB only in migrants from high-prevalence countries.
Medicare subsidises IVF cycles; single embryo transfer is standard practice.

contrast.india: Commercial surrogacy is banned; altruistic only.
contrast.australia: Same principle: only altruistic surrogacy is legal, with state-based rules.

flashcards.front: When to investigate infertility in a 36-year-old woman?
flashcards.back: After 6 months of trying.

flashcards.front: Test that confirms ovulation?
flashcards.back: Mid-luteal serum progesterone, about 7 days before the expected period.

flashcards.front: Why repeat an abnormal semen analysis after about 3 months?
flashcards.back: Spermatogenesis takes about 72 days, and results vary.

flashcards.front: Common male cause of azoospermia seen in gyms?
flashcards.back: Exogenous testosterone or anabolic steroid use.

flashcards.front: Test for tubal patency in primary care referral?
flashcards.back: HyCoSy or hysterosalpingogram (HSG).

flashcards.front: Does AMH predict natural fertility?
flashcards.back: No; it estimates ovarian reserve and response to IVF stimulation.

quiz.stem:
A 37-year-old woman and her 39-year-old male partner attend their GP because they have been trying to conceive for 7 months. Her cycles are regular every 28 days. Neither has had previous children. They are both well.

What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure them and review after 12 months of trying
Begin investigating both partners now
Investigate the woman only; investigate the man if her tests are normal
Start clomiphene citrate
Refer directly for IVF without investigation
quiz.explanation:
Infertility is investigated after 12 months of trying, but after **6 months when the woman is 35 or older**, because fertility falls with age and time matters. She is 37, so investigation should start now.

**Both partners are assessed together**: male factor contributes to a large proportion of cases, and a semen analysis is simple and non-invasive. First-line tests: mid-luteal progesterone, TSH, prolactin, pelvic ultrasound, tubal patency testing, preconception bloods, and a semen analysis. Early referral to a fertility specialist is reasonable given her age.
whyWrong: Waiting 12 months is inappropriate at 37.
Sequential testing wastes time; both partners are investigated together.
Ovulation induction without investigation is inappropriate, especially with regular (likely ovulatory) cycles.
IVF may be needed, but initial assessment guides treatment.

quiz.stem:
A 32-year-old man and his partner have been trying to conceive for 14 months. Her investigations are normal. His semen analysis shows azoospermia. He is a personal trainer and admits injecting testosterone for the past 2 years. Testes are small and soft; the vas deferens is palpable bilaterally.

What is the most likely cause of his azoospermia?
options: Klinefelter syndrome
Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens
Varicocele
Suppression of gonadotrophins by exogenous testosterone
Previous mumps orchitis
quiz.explanation:
**Exogenous testosterone and anabolic steroids** suppress hypothalamic GnRH and pituitary **LH and FSH** through negative feedback. Without FSH and intratesticular testosterone, spermatogenesis stops, causing oligospermia or azoospermia and small, soft testes. Bloods would show **low LH and FSH**.

Management is to stop testosterone; recovery can take many months, and specialist input may be needed. Klinefelter syndrome also causes small testes but with high FSH and LH. The palpable vas deferens argues against congenital absence of the vas.
whyWrong: Klinefelter causes small firm testes with high gonadotrophins; his history gives a clear alternative.
The vas deferens is palpable, excluding congenital absence.
A varicocele reduces sperm quality but rarely causes azoospermia, and none is described.
There is no history of mumps orchitis, and his testosterone use is a clear alternative explanation.

quiz.stem:
A 30-year-old woman has been trying to conceive for 16 months. Her cycles are regular at 28 days. She was treated for pelvic inflammatory disease at 22. Mid-luteal progesterone confirms ovulation; TSH and prolactin are normal. Her partner's semen analysis is normal. Pelvic ultrasound shows a tubular fluid-filled structure next to the right ovary.

Which investigation is most appropriate next?
options: Tubal patency assessment with HyCoSy or HSG
Repeat semen analysis
Serum AMH
Endometrial biopsy
Post-coital test
quiz.explanation:
She ovulates (regular cycles and a mid-luteal progesterone rise), her partner's semen is normal, and she has a history of **PID** with a likely **hydrosalpinx** on ultrasound. **Tubal factor infertility** is the leading suspicion, so the next step is **tubal patency testing** (HyCoSy or HSG, or laparoscopy with dye if other pelvic disease is suspected).

If tubes are blocked, IVF is the usual treatment, and a hydrosalpinx is often removed or clipped first because its fluid reduces implantation rates.
whyWrong: A normal semen analysis does not need repeating in this setting.
AMH estimates ovarian reserve and does not assess tubes.
Endometrial biopsy is not part of routine infertility work-up.
The post-coital test is outdated and not recommended.
